en: And that was when she carried it away.
Hearing the truth, he shouted aloud;
Lion-born Kulchoro
Called his elder, Khan Bakay:
"Akun, it seems, is her father,
And Aychurok is his wife.
Chynkojo, son of Shygay,
Must have stirred up bitter strife.
Unable to endure it, my sister-in-law
Wore her horse's shoulders raw,
Roamed across the whole world,
And must have lost her senses;
She must have carried off Akshunkar,
And so attained her desire.
Saying, 'If he is a man, let him come,'
She must have taken it to Afghanistan.
I heard the plain truth from my sister-in-law;
I heard that Aychurok took it."
Then tiger Bakay,
The saint whose lineage Saint Shay sustained, said:
"What you have said is true.
Akun Khan, the khan of Afghanistan,
And the Bloodthirsty Manas, those two,
Shared the pale star of the heavens
And became friends unto the next world.
They drove livestock as in-laws,
Bowed in homage and tasted fat,
Opened all their hearts to each other,
And had abundant treasure—yellow gold—
Poured down through the roof ring.
They exchanged words of promise
And bound themselves as in-laws."
Tell him to heed the words
Of his elder, old Bakay, without slight;
Tell him to muster Kyrgyz and Argyn,
A mighty, densely gathered host,
A multitude beneath which the earth bends,
And only then set out.
Many there bear claims that breed strife,
And many foes will meet him in battle;
If he will not listen, many enemies await.
Let my only son heed my words:
Many foes lie watching one another.
If my only son has sense,
Let him take his resourceful, wise
Elder Bakay with him;
Whose banner makes men surge,
Who destroys all he encounters;
Let him take the mighty hero Sarykan.
Jamgyrchy will find a way;
Let him take that resourceful hero.
When Manas the Destroyer lived,
We raided Afghanistan and returned once,
And drove them back in disgrace.
On the road leading to Afghanistan
There stands Kambyl-Bel,
And there is the pass of Belendi,
And a desert two days wide,
And a people wild beyond measure.
For slaughtering the giants
Janaaly and Karach side by side,
They harbor vengeance along that road."
When Kulchoro heard this,
He spoke to Kanchoro,
Uttering an astonishing thought no man could know:
"Ah, uncle Kanchoro!
Does a mortal man not die?
Must this borrowed, fleeting soul not see
What God has laid upon one's head?
Khan Bakay has grown old,
Jamgyrchy is aged,
Sarykan's time has passed,
And Bolokbay will be burdened.
If they were goods for the bride-price,
Why lead the old men with us?
What desire shall we attain,
We, all sons of khans,
To Opol standing here
Will go ourselves.
If we return, there will be trouble:
We have beaten his wife and left her.
We shall take your Bloodthirsty Manas with us
And travel onward from there."
Having settled it thus, Kulchoro
In Kanykey's encampment
Prepared a deep blue-green saddlebag.
"If an enemy comes out shooting,
He will be left powerless," he said;
The saddlebag held abundant powder and shot.
He had it folded and made ready
And loaded upon Akborchuk.
A great golden tent for sleeping,
A bronze field cauldron for cooking,
And six grooms to tend the horses—
Exactly twenty-five souls in all—
Were setting out for Afghanistan.
Driving fourteen horses from Talas,
Akborchuk bore the provisions,
And Kokborchuk carried the liquor.
Driving fourteen horses from Ogoy,
These young men, seeking their lord,
Spurred eagerly and rode hard.
They had their equipment folded,
And all their armor and weapons
Loaded upon fourteen horses,
With ample food and ammunition.
Your dear mother Kanykey
Had made for the fourteen horses
Special white ammunition cases,
Each fitted to its horse.
The young men eagerly drove them hard,
And to their lord, lofty as Opol Mountain,
Their hearts opened in gladness;
Before their elder's eyes
They appeared like an army of six divisions.
Kanchoro and Kulchoro
Raced side by side,
Their stirrups striking together,
And before their elder
They came proclaiming good news:
"Ah, elder brother, a reward for good news!
Akun Khan is your father-in-law,
And Aychurok is your wife.
Aychurok, daughter of Akun,
Changed herself into a white swan.
She listened closely to your words,
And took a great liking to you.
When she rose over the ridge,
My hero, she reached you;
But after speaking sternly with your wife,
She departed deeply offended.
She changed herself into a white swan
And scattered her venomous fury.
To the city of Akun Khan,
Saying, 'Let him seek and find her,'
She carried Akshunkar away!
If you are a man, my heroic elder,
Churok of old and the falcon—
Let us find a way to seek and recover them.
If you are still a mere boy, come,
Let us go back to your wife.
If it is true that you are a hero,
Dear elder, come and ride with us;
Let us cast turmoil across the world!
If a seething host of enemies comes out,
Let us charge and level our spears;
Let us turn and fight without fleeing,
And rest only when we have won Aychurok.
Your encampment stands settled in Talas;
We would be less than men if we did not take
Your wife named Aychurok.
While your fortune remains unharmed,
Elder, your fortune is like
The shoulder of a mountain.
Do not let people say, 'Semetey, son of Manas,
Had his falcon carried away,
And Semetey, out of fear,
Let his falcon be taken
And failed even to notice.'
Driving fourteen horses from the Kyrgyz,
Let us follow the winding road.
My blessed elder, heed my words;
Let us overtake your maiden bride!
If we prove unworthy, let us die;
Rather than walk the earth alive,
Let us sink away as though never born!
Only now have I heard your story,
And of the wife your father,
Tiger Manas, appointed for you.
You have girded your waist for action;
Now tighten that girdle more firmly.
My heroic elder, stand and hear
The words your young men have brought you!
Your wife proved black-hearted;
She did not know how to honor guests.
She reviled tiger Bakay and exposed
The private affairs of the three khans one by one.
With hero Bakay at their head,
Your three khans sat there abashed,
Their heads hanging like howling dogs.
In fury she hemmed her in;
My dear mother Kanykey
And beat her with a staff.
The beating brought her to submission;
Your two companions exhausted themselves,
For formidable indeed, heroic one,
Was the trouble caused by your wife.
Your noble elder is a khan;
We began the uproar,
And beat your broad-rumped wife
More than a little!
We brought calamity down upon her head,
And, making her cry out beneath our blows,
Forced her to tell of Akshunkar!
If you would have us struck down, Opol lies here;
If you say, 'They touched my wife,'
And have a hero cut us down, here we stand!
Here stands the governed Argyn people;
If you say, 'They caused this disaster,'
And cut off our heads, here we stand!
Young sultan, you now know our news:
Though we pleaded, she ranted on,
And your wife hurled many insults.
For beating your wife and leaving her,
The blame belongs to us, your two companions!
Judge fully which side behaved wantonly;
Poor lord, listen to us—
If you would destroy us, here we stand!
If you send us, the road of the journey is here;
If you pour out your fury, lord, here we stand!"
The young lord was a tiger,
A saint born greater still
Than his father, gray-maned Manas.
He hung close around his neck
The gray purse left by Manas.
That poor lion, speaking timidly,
Appealed to his young men;
Showing that he was their lord,
He placed Kulchoro on his right,
And Kanchoro on his left,
He seated both upon his knees,
His mind filled with boundless thoughts,
And fondled the young men:
"My matched pair of lions,
While your heroic elder still has life,
For the two boys left among the khans
Like crows upon
A stake of black steel,
It is not merely my wife, young men—
My own dark life is yours in sacrifice!
Young men, leave my kinsman and take my household;
Leave the two of us and take the one;
Leave my wealth and take my encampment;
If you wish, take the wife you struck!"
Raging and distraught,
He pleaded with the two servants.
When he heard what had happened to the falcon,
He shouted, "Baabedin!"
And raised the battle cry, "Manas!"
Semetey rejoiced greatly,
As though his gray-maned father,
Tiger Manas, had returned to life.
He had a pale white mare caught
And sacrificed beneath the crescent hoof.
Semetey hurried with all his might,
Your hero, born more precious
Than Manas of the forty holy companions,
A hero who took after
His father, gray-maned Manas, without deviation.
The tent with golden cords
He had folded splendidly;
Striped felt and provisions
He had loaded upon Akborchuk.
He took a barren three-year-old horse for slaughter,
Rich fat for their provisions,
And red tea for their drink.
